{"id": "33:42/q06", "question": "Why is tasbīḥ singled out after remembrance?", "turns_on": "The distinction depends on whether tasbīḥ is a special form of spoken remembrance, an especially important prayer, or optional prayer.", "positions": [{"id": "33:42/q06/p1", "position": "It is a central or especially excellent form of remembrance.", "reasons": "Kashshāf says singling it out marks special merit; Bayḍāwī calls it the core of remembrance. Nasafī compares Gabriel and Michael singled out among angels and links its merit to denying unworthy attributes. Bursevī calls it the central adornment; Elmalılı likewise calls it central. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the formula comprehensively praises God and denies imperfections."}, {"id": "33:42/q06/p2", "position": "Prayer is singled out as the specially timed form of general remembrance.", "reasons": "Kashshāf says all good deeds may be dhikr, with prayers excelling them. Abū Ḥayyān singles prayer out of all obedience, while Islahi says constant remembrance is general and set prayer times the specific. Kuran Yolu finds the second command probably refers to prayers."}, {"id": "33:42/q06/p3", "position": "If it means optional prayer, it is not a specific instance within general remembrance.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr distinguishes this possible reading from the verbal formula reading."}]}
{"id": "33:42/q07", "question": "Who may recite these remembrances, and in what state?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "33:42/q07/p1", "position": "People in ritual purity, minor impurity, or major impurity may recite the formulas.", "reasons": "Mujāhid includes all three states. Baghawī and Qurṭubī repeat the view. Bursevī cites a hadith urging even the person in major impurity not to omit transcendence, praise, oneness and greatness; he infers the same even more strongly for minor impurity. Purity and ablution remain proper etiquette."}]}
{"id": "33:42/q08", "question": "What reported benefits or practices accompany morning, evening, or repeated glorification?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "33:42/q08/p1", "position": "Those who remember and glorify God can have the angels pray for them.", "reasons": "Sulaym ibn ʿĀmir reports a man's dream of angels praying at every movement; Abū Umāma cites 33:41–42 as the means. reports this from Muʿādh ibn Anas, Ibn Mardawayh and Jābir."}, {"id": "33:42/q08/p6", "position": "The Prophet commended the accessible formula Subḥān Allāh wa-bi-ḥamdihī.", "reasons": "The report describes the expression as two near or readily accessible words, as excerpted."}, {"id": "33:42/q08/p7", "position": "A hundred daily repetitions of Subḥān Allāh wa-bi-ḥamdihī erase sins even as "reasons": "The Prophet gives this answer to a question about earning a thousand good deeds in one day."}, {"id": "33:42/q08/p9", "position": "The phrase 'Allāhu akbar kabīran wa-subḥānallāhi bukratan wa-aṣīlā' can replace counting glorifications with pebbles or seeds.", "reasons": "ʿAbdallāh advises a Hamdānī woman who counted her recitations with such objects."}, {"id": "33:42/q08/p10", "position": "Dawn prayer followed by remembrance until sunrise and two rakʿahs earns a complete ḥajj and ʿumra reward three times over.", "reasons": "Bursevī reports the hadith."}, {"id": "33:42/q08/p11", "position": "Sleeping before sunrise and certain grave acts make the earth cry out.", "reasons": "Bursevī reports a tradition coupling sleeping then with unlawful bloodshed and bathing after fornication."}, {"id": "33:42/q08/p12", "position": "Sufi practitioners gather for remembrance after dawn until sunrise prayer.", "reasons": "Bursevī says this remembrance acts powerfully on the soul and is preferred to recitation at that time."}, {"id": "33:42/q08/p13", "position": "Blessings on the Prophet, supplication and tasbīḥ are preferred to recitation while prayer {"id": "33:42/q09", "question": "How does this command relate to the surrounding passage and other verses?", "turns_on": "The notes variously connect the command to its preceding controversy, the following promise, and parallel verses.", "positions": [{"id": "33:42/q09/p1", "position": "Other verses name or prescribe comparable times of glorification and prayer.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr cites 30:17–18 for evening, morning and other day periods; Study Quran cites the same pair and 6:52, 18:28, 19:11, 24:36, 48:9 for persistent devotion. Islahi points to 17:78 and 20:130 for prayer times and 2:45 for prayer's tie to perseverance."}, {"id": "33:42/q09/p2", "position": "It redirects believers from conflict with hypocrites over the Prophet to remembrance.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says replacing argument or insult over rumors about the Prophet's marriage to Zaynab avoids civic strife; he compares remembrance replacing tribal boasting after pilgrimage (2:200) and restraint from provoking retaliation against God (6:108). It follows the instruction to the Prophet to leave harm aside (33:48); continued dispute would mark disobedient hypocrites. The new address remains contextually connected. Islahi likewise urges disregarding the hypocrites' uproar and praising God by night and day."}, {"id": "33:42/q09/p3", "position": "The next verse promises divine and angelic blessings to those who remember.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr connects the practice to 33:43; Ibn ʿAbbās, as reported by al-Ṭabarī, says God and the angels then pray for those who remember in every condition."}]}
{"id": "33:42/q10", "question": "What does the remembrance urged here accomplish for the believer?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "33:42/q10/p1", "position": "It establishes servitude and sustains the believer's awareness of God.", "reasons": "Abū al-Ḥusayn ibn Hind says God calls and selects believers through the Prophet, directs them to unity and commands servitude; remembrance establishes that servitude. Kuran Yolu calls tongue and heart remembrance, reflection and awareness the energy and lifeline of servitude."}, {"id": "33:42/q10/p2", "position": "It brings God's and the angels' blessings.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr cites the following verse 33:43; Ibn ʿAbbās says remembrance has no fixed limit and its practitioners receive these blessings."}, {"id": "33:42/q10/p3", "position": "It shields believers and supports perseverance against enemies.", "reasons": "Islahi calls remembrance a shield against Satan and links calls to persevere with prayer, referring to the discussion of 2:45."}, {"id": "33:42/q10/p4", "position": "It gives the soul a powerful response to devotion at dawn.", "reasons": "Bursevī says Sufi remembrance after dawn until the sunrise prayer strongly affects the soul."}]}
{"id": "33:42/q11", "question": "What inward images are attached to remembering or glorifying God here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "33:42/q11/p1", "position": "Remembrance can be the unbroken awareness of one who never forgets God.", "reasons": "Sulamī cites an anonymous poem whose speaker says remembrance is unnecessary because God is never forgotten."}, {"id": "33:42/q11/p2", "position": "Love's remembrance is death and renewed life through longing and hope.", "reasons": "ʿAlī ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥīm's verses make love life through hope and death through longing; inexhaustible love never forgets the beloved."}, {"id": "33:42/q11/p3", "position": "The heart's dawn begins as the lower self's darkness recedes, leading to enduring annihilation.", "reasons": "Qāshānī depicts a heart lit at morning and the spirit's sun setting in annihilation of Essence; remembrance continues to everlasting annihilation."}, {"id": "33:42/q11/p4", "position": "Spiritual attraction reveals divine light even as created lamps fade.", "reasons": "Bursevī's Persian lines say the inwardly perceptive see an eternal sun in an atom and a sea in a drop; another couplet urges familiarity with love's sea and purity like a shell. He prays for spiritual acts that bring blessings and meet needs."}]}
{"id": "33:42/q12", "question": "Why is morning named before aṣīl here, while 30:17 begins with evening?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "33:42/q12/p1", "position": "Morning naturally precedes afternoon; 30:17 follows a different calendrical starting point.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says this verse simply follows the day's order with no special foregrounding of aṣīl. In 30:17 evening includes early night, which begins a day in the Arab and Islamic reckoning of a month."}]}

{"id": "33:42/q14", "question": "Where is the fuller lexical discussion of aṣīl in al-Wāḥidī's commentary?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "33:42/q14/p1", "position": "Under the phrase bi-l-ghuduww wa-l-āṣāl.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī refers the reader there."}]}
{"id": "34:10/q01", "question": "Who is David, and what is said of his name?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "34:10/q01/p1", "position": "His foreign name may be linked to the phrase 'he healed his wound.'", "reasons": "Qushayri gives both accounts; Bursevi reads the absence of connecting letters in the name as a sign of detachment from the world, hidden and manifest grace, and divinely bestowed names."}, {"id": "34:10/q01/p2", "position": "David is the Israelite prophet.", "reasons": "Kur’an Yolu identifies him from the Qur'an and Bible, citing 2:251 and 27:15."}]}
{"id": "34:10/q02", "question": "What is the favor given to David?", "turns_on": "Whether faḍl identifies a particular gift, gathers his gifts, or describes a distinction in rank.", "positions": [{"id": "34:10/q02/p1", "position": "Prophethood, often together with the Psalms or revelation.", "reasons": "Muqatil cites 4:113; Wahidi reports Muqatil's prophecy and scripture and Kalbi's prophecy plus worldly gifts. Study Quran cites 4:163. Tabrisī adds decisive judgment and miracles."}, {"id": "34:10/q02/p2", "position": "A comprehensive divine gift, exceptionally great but not necessarily superiority in every respect.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbas says none before or after got the like. Baydawi considers superiority over prophets or all people; Alusi reports rankings over earlier prophets, Israelite prophets, all except Muhammad, or all prophets, and questions uniqueness of kingship and voice. Bursevi cites 2:253 and allows advantage in one respect amid inferiority in another. Kur'an Yolu permits a simple 'favor' with no claim of superiority."}, {"id": "34:10/q02/p3", "position": "His beautiful voice, sweet prayer, good character, and intimacy.", "reasons": "Sulami's Nahrajuri stresses sweet intimate prayer. Qushayri lists voice, prayer, character and justice. Qurtubi cites 35:1, the Prophet's praise of Abu Musa's 'flute of David,' and the scholars' explanation of mizmar as voice."}, {"id": "34:10/q02/p4", "position": "Subjection and response of mountains and birds.", "reasons": "Mawardi lists this favor; Qushayri says their response consoled David in grief; Qurtubi also mentions people. Bursevi includes pliable iron, Psalms and miracles."}, {"id": "34:10/q02/p5", "position": "Just judgment, discernment, intelligence, or knowledge.", "reasons": "Qurtubi cites 27:15 for knowledge and 38:26 for just rule; Study Quran cites 21:79 and 27:15."}, {"id": "34:10/q02/p6", "position": "Strength, kingship, soft iron, armor craft and other worldly gifts.", "reasons": "Qurtubi cites 38:17 for strength and separately lists iron; Wahidi reports Kalbi's worldly gifts. Ibn Ashur enumerates courage, reform, self-support, long life and more; Kur'an Yolu adds reconciliation."}, {"id": "34:10/q02/p7", "position": "David's repentance and return to God.", "reasons": "Qurtubi cites 38:25. Qushayri says humility and apology followed his lapse; Sulami's account presents return after a stumble."}, {"id": "34:10/q02/p8", "position": "The Psalms themselves.", "reasons": "Mawardi and Qurtubi give this separately; Abu Hayyan lists them among David's gifts."}, {"id": "34:10/q02/p9", "position": "Reliance on God and awareness of utter need.", "reasons": "Sulami's Ibn ʿAta says the servant has no good apart from God in obedience or sin; Jaʿfar says trust and reliance; Ibn Khallal says knowing one's measure and returning. Qushayri reports David's awareness of need."}, {"id": "34:10/q02/p10", "position": "Mercy for the weak and love for the poor.", "reasons": "Sulami transmits ʿAbd al-ʿAziz; Mawardi lists mercy."}]}
{"id": "34:10/q03", "question": "What does 'from Us' and the indefinite 'favor' convey?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "34:10/q03/p1", "position": "The favor originates directly from God and its indefinite form magnifies it.", "reasons": "Razi says 'from Us' marks special prophetic rank despite general favors, citing 9:21. Biqai denies any independent created source. Alusi says beneficence is magnified and fronted for focus and anticipation, citing 18:65. Ibn Ashur says min denotes origin governed by ātaynā, citing 28:57; he lists David's gifts."}, {"id": "34:10/q03/p2", "position": "Ātaynā simply means 'We gave'; faḍl is a gift or increase.", "reasons": "Qurtubi says faḍl distinguishes David above others; Tabatabai says gift; Bursevi says increase."}]}
{"id": "34:10/q04", "question": "How is the call to the mountains connected syntactically to the gift?", "turns_on": "Whether the quoted call apposes the gift or giving, or begins with an implied saying.", "positions": [{"id": "34:10/q04/p1", "position": "An omitted 'We said' introduces the quoted command, explaining the favor.", "reasons": "Yahya says God called the mountains. Kashshaf, Razi, Baydawi, Nasafi and Abu Hayyan allow apposition to faḍlan or ātaynā; Ibn Ashur calls omission of the speech verb common and sees the clause as explanation. Wahidi reports Abu Ubayda and Zajjaj's ellipsis."}]}
{"id": "34:10/q05", "question": "What does 'awwibī with him' ask the mountains to do?", "turns_on": "Arabic return and repetition, daytime travel, practical compliance, echo of lament, or Ethiopian glorification.", "positions": [{"id": "34:10/q05/p1", "position": "Repeat or return David's praise and glorification of God.", "reasons": "Mujahid, Ibn ʿAbbas, Qatada and others gloss it 'glorify'; Tabari adduces return and a poet; Zajjaj, Tabrisī and Ibn Kathir derive repetition from āba. Wahidi reports exegetical consensus and Ibn Qutayba's alternative. 38:18–19 and 21:79 support praise. Alusi prefers Arabic taʾwīb; Ibn Kathir prefers this contextual sense. Islahi defines joining another's tune."}, {"id": "34:10/q05/p2", "position": "Travel with David by day, returning to the journey until night.", "reasons": "Hasan and Jubba'i take movement literally; Ibn Qutayba and Abu Amr define taʾwīb as daylong travel and night rest. Ibn Muqbil and Salama b. Jandal supply poems. Ibn Kathir calls it remote; Alusi objects that mountains are earth's pegs and no travel report exists; Tabatabai cites the parallel praise passage against it."}, {"id": "34:10/q05/p3", "position": "Echo David's sorrowful lament or recitation.", "reasons": "Nahhas says mountains answered his Psalms; Wahb says they echoed lament and birds gathered. Qushayri places David grieving in mountains and wilderness; Kashshaf says lament for sin. Alusi and Abu Hayyan object that ordinary echo is not truly the mountain's act or a distinctive miracle."}, {"id": "34:10/q05/p4", "position": "The word itself means 'glorify' in Abyssinian or Ethiopian.", "reasons": "Abu Maysara and Muʾarrij transmit this foreign-language gloss; Ibn ʿAtiyya calls it weak and unrecognized; Ibn Kathir questions it; Alusi favors the Arabic derivation."}, {"id": "34:10/q05/p5", "position": "Comply with David's actions or aims, including practical works.", "reasons": "Tabrisi specifies wells, springs, ore and roads; Abu Hayyan reports the Psalms and birds listening. Alusi objects that Arabic taʾwīb does not cover varied actions."}, {"id": "34:10/q05/p6", "position": "Prompt David to praise by his contemplation of them.", "reasons": "Alusi rejects this as contrary to transmitted glosses and 'with him,' and as no special miracle."}]}
{"id": "34:10/q06", "question": "How is 'awwibī' read and formed?", "turns_on": "Doubled wāw from taʾwīb versus light wāw from awb; whether doubling is intensive or causative.", "positions": [{"id": "34:10/q06/p1", "position": "A light wāw with ḍamma on hamza reads 'return with him' from awb.", "reasons": "Hasan, Qatada, Ibn Abi Ishaq, Ibn Abbas and others are named; Zajjaj allows return to praise. Tabari rejects an alternative as contrary to authoritative readers."}, {"id": "34:10/q06/p2", "position": "The common reading doubles wāw, from taʾwīb, expressing repeated or caused return of praise.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan argues that doubling makes intransitive āba transitive, against Ibn ʿAtiyya's intensive analysis. Razi and Kashshaf list both forms."}]}
{"id": "34:10/q07", "question": "Why is the imperative to the mountains feminine singular?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "34:10/q07/p1", "position": "A nonrational plural regularly takes feminine singular agreement.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAtiyya compares a call to horses and 20:18; Abu Hayyan cites poetic horse calls and notes rare extension to rational feminine plurals; Alusi adds a poetic command to women."}]}
{"id": "34:10/q08", "question": "How did the mountains' response occur?", "turns_on": "A created audible voice versus natural echo, distinct glorification, or another mechanism.", "positions": [{"id": "34:10/q08/p1", "position": "God enabled real, audible glorification by the mountains as David glorified.", "reasons": "Kashshaf compares speech created in the tree; Tabrisī allows created praise and understanding; Qurtubi calls it a miracle. Alusi adduces pebbles heard in the hands of the Prophet and Abu Bakr. Biqai adds pebbles, food, greeting stone, moaning trunk, lizard and camel reports, and argues that birds' own speech excludes mere echo. Abu Hayyan notes the Muʿtazilite implication of the tree analogy."}, {"id": "34:10/q08/p2", "position": "The mountain sound was an echo of David's chanting.", "reasons": "Thaʿlabi and Ibn ʿAtiyya report this as the origin of mountain echoes; Baghawi and Wahidi also describe birds gathering overhead. Wahb says their response supported David when he faltered."}, {"id": "34:10/q08/p3", "position": "God caused mountains to move physically with David.", "reasons": "Jubba'i considers it a miracle; Alusi denies any re

Qushayri says the response consoled grief."}, {"id": "34:10/q08/p5", "position": "The mountains retained their own distinct praise while joining David.", "reasons": "Bursevi says true unveiling hears a separate remembrance from each thing; their cooperation need not erase that. {"id": "34:10/q09", "question": "Why address mountains and birds as though they could understand?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "34:10/q09/p1", "position": "The vivid command displays God's sovereignty and David's stature by portraying even hard mountains and fleeing birds as obedient.", "reasons": "Kashshaf says this is more majestic than plain narration; Razi says stone and birds make the miracle striking and hardened human hearts worse. Biqai sees earthly and heavenly signs in hardest mountains and light birds; Ibn Ashur calls the address a creative command and notes the compact majesty of 'with him.'"}]}
{"id": "34:10/q10", "question": "How is 'the birds' read and parsed?", "turns_on": "Whether nominative or accusative, and which word or implied construction governs it.", "positions": [{"id": "34:10/q10/p1", "position": "The accusative coordinates with the vocative's underlying syntactic position: birds too are called.", "reasons": "Sibawayh, Zajjaj, Tabari and others invoke the accusative position of vocatives; ʿIsa ibn ʿUmar reads it so. Some grammarians object that a definite noun cannot be vocative, answered by dependent-form syntax. Yunus, Abu Amr and others prefer accusative in such coordination; Jishumi's Ali ibn Isa prefers another surface-based analysis."}, {"id": "34:10/q10/p2", "position": "The nominative joins the surface vocative 'mountains,' so birds are also addressed.", "reasons": "Attested by al-Aʿraj, Yaʿqub, Ubayd ibn Umayr, Abu Razin, Ibn Hurmuz and others; Baydawi and Alusi note that the vocative ending resembles inflection. Tabari cites 21:79 and a poetic call to ʿAmr and Dahhak."}, {"id": "34:10/q10/p3", "position": "The accusative follows an omitted verb: 'We subjected' or 'We gave the birds.'", "reasons": "Abu Amr and Ibn Zayd supply the verb; Tabari cites 21:79. Jishumi adduces a poetic omission for watering. Grammarians also propose 'I mean.'"}, {"id": "34:10/q10/p4", "position": "The accusative coordinates with faḍlan or ātaynā: birds are part of God's gift.", "reasons": "Kisa'i and Abu Amr argue giving birds means subjecting them. Farra compares 'I fed him food and gave him water'; Tibi adds straw and water poetry. Bursevi denies need for an omitted verb or noun, against al-Irshad; Kisa'i elsewhere supplies 'their glorification.'"}, {"id": "34:10/q10/p5", "position": "The accusative is comitative: the birds accompany the mountains' response.", "reasons": "Zajjaj compares 'I stood with Zayd'; Nahhas gives water with wood. Wahidi prefers this among Abu Ishaq's parses. Abu Hayyan objects that maʿahu already fills the role; Khafaji replies it may be an adverb, while Alusi rejects a further defense based on omitted conjunction or delayed relation."}, {"id": "34:10/q10/p6", "position": "The nominative coordinates with the subject pronoun in 'awwibī,' making birds join the action.", "reasons": "Zajjaj, Tabari and others give this analysis; Nahhas and Alusi say maʿahu separates the verb and noun sufficiently. Abu Hayyan also offers a new subject with omitted predicate."}]}
{"id": "34:10/q11", "question": "What did the birds do with David?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "34:10/q11/p1", "position": "They joined his glorification and answered him, sometimes gathering or circling above.", "reasons": "Ibn Zayd and Ibn Abbas report praise; Ibn Jawzi adds listeners weeping. Wahb has David call mountains to glorify, birds to answer, then chant Psalms; Ibn Kathir says birds stopped and answered in varied languages. Qurtubi says wild animals gathered and water stopped to listen; Wahb as transmitted by Ibn Kathir mentions seventy vocal tones and imitators' instruments."}, {"id": "34:10/q11/p2", "position": "In one reported aftermath, the birds dispersed when David's state changed after repentance.", "reasons": "Qushayri says his voice was familiar but birds left because his lapse had caused estrangement, whereas earlier obedience brought intimacy; he says the spiritual meaning belonged to David, not the creatures."}]}
{"id": "34:10/q12", "question": "What does softening the iron mean?", "turns_on": "Physical pliability, David's strength or skill, ordinary smelting, symbolic sharpness, or inward allegory.", "positions": [{"id": "34:10/q12/p1", "position": "God made iron physically pliable in David's hand like wax, dough, wet clay, or threads.", "reasons": "Muqatil says he plaited it; Yahya says three fingers sufficed. Qatada, Hasan and others say no heating or hammering. Farra says it flowed. Ibn Ashur specifies rings and rivets; he also describes ordinary heated iron. Razi argues fire already melts iron, making the miracle conceivable. Elmalili rejects reduction to ordinary discovery. Asad allows literal iron as one reading."}, {"id": "34:10/q12/p2", "position": "Iron was easy for David to bend because God gave him extraordinary strength.", "reasons": "Mawardi says it kept its nature, comparing pliability in human dealings; Baydawi permits either mechanism. Bursevi cites 38:17 and says David was strong but not bulky. Kur'an Yolu prefers adequate strength and special skill in light of 34:11."}, {"id": "34:10/q12/p3", "position": "The phrase refers to David's discovery or development of ironworking and armor craft.", "reasons": "Elmalili reports and rejects a reduction to extraction and melting with tools, yet allows David to have refined known smelting into thin armor. Kur'an Yolu prefers divine direction, strength and skill; Islahi stresses light protective mail."}, {"id": "34:10/q12/p4", "position": "Inwardly, softened iron is David's softened heart or elemental bodily nature.", "reasons": "Qashani identifies bodily nature; Bursevi transmits Najmi's image of the softened heart and armor as profound judgments voiced from it."}, {"id": "34:10/q12/p5", "position": "Al-ḥadīd can mean sharpness, whose softening alludes to David's gentle aesthetic and moral character.", "reasons": "Asad cites 50:22 and idioms of sharp intellect, sight and odor; definite al-ḥadīd permits sharpness or iron. His interpretation points to Psalms, goodness and humility."}]}
{"id": "34:10/q13", "question": "Why was iron softened and how did David use it?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "34:10/q13/p1", "position": "He made coats of linked mail, becoming the first to do so rather than using older iron plates.", "reasons": "Zajjaj and Qatada contrast mail with earlier cuirasses or plates. Muqatil says a suit took part of a day or night and fetched 1,000 dirhams; another report says a suit fetched 4,000; another says one daily fetched 6,000, with 2,000 for family and 4,000 for Israelite poor. Ibn Ashur describes rings and rivets. 21:80 says armor protects people in battle and, for Elmalili, its address suggests transmission to Muhammad's community. Razi says protective armor preserves life, better than swords or arrows; Abu Hayyan contrasts David's armor with Solomon's peaceful buildings. Al-Biqāʿī connects the emphatic warning to denials of resurrection and divine attributes."}]}
{"id": "34:11/q21", "question": "What inward meanings are drawn from the armor and its measured links?", "turns_on": "Whether the symbolic measure governs inner moral craft or the delivery of wisdom.", "positions": [{"id": "34:11/q21/p1", "position": "The armor is scrupulous piety and its linked construction is practical wisdom guarding against the soul and Satan.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī reads the protective garment as piety, the arrows as hostile impulses, and measured linking as skilled rational and religious practice that purifies deeds."}, {"id": "34:11/q21/p2", "position": "Measured linking means speaking wisdom in amounts listeners can grasp.", "reasons": "Al-Būrsawī transmits Taʾwīlāt al-Najmiyya and cites a Persian couplet warning against scattering jewels of wisdom before a donkey."}]}
{"id": "34:11/q22", "question": "Who is addressed in the inward reading of 'do good'?", "turns_on": "The inward readings differ in symbolic referent and emphasis.", "positions": [{"id": "34:11/q22/p1", "position": "David signifies the spirit and its faculties; those working for God ascend through righteous deeds.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī says the workers gather from the lower realm toward the upper, preparing for holy lights."}, {"id": "34:11/q22/p2", "position": "Every outward and inward faculty must perform its created act of servitude.", "reasons": "Al-Būrsawī reports the Taʾwīlāt al-Najmiyya reading."}]}
{"id": "34:11/q23", "question": "What special effect is ascribed to reciting the name al-Baṣīr?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "34:11/q23/p1", "position": "Reciting it one hundred times before Friday prayer opens inward sight and guides speech and action.", "reasons": "Al-Būrsawī reports this special effect of the divine name, while acknowledging human fallibility."}]}
{"id": "34:11/q24", "question": "What story about David's lapse is told here?", "turns_on": "The two reports focus on different consequences of David's lapse.", "positions": [{"id": "34:11/q24/p1", "position": "After his own lapse, David changed from asking that wrongdoers not be forgiven to praying for their forgiveness.", "reasons": "Al-Būrsawī transmits the saying as a lesson about zeal, fault and mercy."}, {"id": "34:11/q24/p2", "position": "After David repented, birds heard his voice but withdrew because his lapse had altered their intimacy with him.", "reasons": "Al-Būrsawī reports God explaining their estrangement as the effect of disobedience."}]}
{"id": "34:11/q25", "question": "How is gratitude construed in the nearby command to work?", "turns_on": "Whether shukran intensifies the act of thanking or states the purpose of obedient work.", "positions": [{"id": "34:11/q25/p1", "position": "Shukran is a cognate accusative: 'give thanks, thanking.'", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī gives this analysis of the following gratitude wording."}, {"id": "34:11/q25/p2", "position": "Shukran expresses purpose, with obedience understood as the object of 'do.'", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī offers this as the alternative parse of the following gratitude wording."}]}
{"id": "34:11/q26", "question": "How is David's softened iron compared with the Prophet's miracles?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "34:11/q26/p1", "position": "It is set beside transformations of a trench rock, wooden objects into swords, and a severed hand restored.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī cites the trench rock's breaking in one account and becoming loose sand with water in another; Salmān's report has three illuminating blows and announced conquests. He also cites reports on ʿAbd Allāh b. Jaḥsh, ʿUkāsha, Salama b. Aslam, and Muʿawwidh b. ʿAfrāʾ."}]}
{"id": "34:11/q27", "question": "How does the armor instruction relate to other verses?", "turns_on": "The notes connect the verse to protective craft, the surrounding account of favors, and the sūrah's warning.", "positions": [{"id": "34:11/q27/p1", "position": "Qur'an 21:80 describes armor making as protection and extends its benefit to Muhammad's community.", "reasons": "Elmalılı and Kur'an Yolu use that verse to explain defense and the community's inherited craft."}, {"id": "34:11/q27/p2", "position": "The command belongs to the sequence of favors to David and Solomon and the call to grateful work.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī sees armor making as the purpose of softened iron and as work devoted to God; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī lists mountains, birds, iron, wind and obedient jinn. Study Quran says this follows criticism of disbelievers."}, {"id": "34:11/q27/p3", "position": "David and Solomon's grateful rule contrasts with affluent Quraysh and Sheba, and points from worldly reward to resurrection.", "reasons": "Islāḥī says David and Solomon remained grateful, unlike arrogant Quraysh; the Sheba example shows wrath, and present reward and punishment challenge denial of the next life."}]}
{"id": "34:11/q28", "question": "What is said about the sūrah's place of revelation?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "34:11/q28/p1", "position": "Sūrat Sabaʾ is Makkan.", "reasons": "Study Quran's introduction states this."}]}
{"id": "35:18/q01", "question": "What does wizr mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "35:18/q01/p1", "position": "A heavy load, here sin and its liability or punishment.", "reasons": "Jishumī gives the plural awzār and calls sins heavy; Kashshāf, Nasafī, and Ibn ʿĀshūr compare wiqr; Māwardī connects wazīr with bearing a ruler's burden; al-Rāghib distinguishes wazr refuge from wizr burden; Elmalılı stresses punishment."}, {"id": "35:18/q01/p2", "position": "The root verb means to carry a load.", "reasons": "Bursevī gives wazara-yaziru and wazara-yūzaru; Ibn ʿAṭiyya glosses taziru as carrying."}]}
{"id": "35:18/q02", "question": "What does the first clause teach?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "35:18/q02/p1", "position": "Each soul bears only its own sin and is not punished for another's deed.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī and many others state divine justice; Zamakhsharī, Abū Ḥayyān, Bursevī, and Biqāʿī contrast worldly tyrants. Abū Rimtha reports the Prophet applying it to father and son; ʿAmr ibn al-Aḥwaṣ reports his Farewell Pilgrimage statement."}, {"id": "35:18/q02/p2", "position": "It covers duties as well as sins.", "reasons": "Study Quran reports Aj, IK, R, and Ṭ with this broader expression."}]}
{"id": "35:18/q03", "question": "Why use wāzirah rather than simply nafs?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "35:18/q03/p1", "position": "It depicts a soul already carrying its own burden and makes the negated rule general.", "reasons": "Rāzī says a bare 'soul' could imply a soul with no burden; Nasafī and Biqāʿī stress its existing load. A reported scholar says the participle denotes an established quality, indefinite under negation. Ālūsī rejects a need for grammatical tajrīd."}, {"id": "35:18/q03/p2", "position": "It foregrounds the soul as the one that earns and bears its deeds.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr cites 6:164 and 74:38."}]}
